extracted.intended_audience: classical scholars, editors, translators, and students of Latin literature
extracted.subtask_description: Preparing, editing, annotating, or interpreting Horace's Satires: including assessing manuscripts, using scholia, establishing text, and commenting on style, theme, and influence for scholarly publication or study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript class evaluation (Class I vs Class II)
rubrics_metrics.description: one of which stands out as conspicuous for accuracy. Yet, as a group, the mss. of Class I. are distinctly superior to those of Class II., though not infrequently the latter preserve correct readings which the former had lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Class I manuscripts as generally superior overall but examine Class II as well because they may preserve correct or otherwise valuable readings lost in Class I. Weigh individual readings against internal and external evidence rather than assuming blanket superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and limits of Horatian scholia (Porphyrio and Acron)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collections of Horatian scholia, or explanatory notes, have come down to us ... Both collections are largely interpolated. Both, however, precede our mss. in point of time, and are therefore valuable in determining the priority of conflicting readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Porphyrio and Acron as early witnesses for establishing the priority of variant readings, but be cautious because the scholia are 'largely interpolated'—assess individual scholia for plausibility and possible later additions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of marginalia/Commentator Cruquianus
rubrics_metrics.description: The term Commentator Cruquianus is given to a collection of notes gathered by Cruquius from the marginalia in his Blandinian mss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider marginal notes (as compiled under names like 'Commentator Cruquianus') as potential sources of variant readings or interpretive notes; trace provenance (which manuscripts provided the marginalia) and evaluate reliability before adopting conjectures from them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive bibliographic consultation for editors
rubrics_metrics.description: There are also many pamphlets and periodical articles, too numerous to record, which must be consulted by an editor of Horace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When editing Horace, consult a wide bibliography—editions (editio princeps, Bentley, Heinsius, later standard editions), monographs, articles, and pamphlets. Recognize edition-history milestones (e.g., editio princeps c.1470; Bentley as an epoch) and check secondary literature for past conjectures and arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document and weigh textual variants and conjectures
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnotes and apparatus cite variant readings and conjectures (e.g., 'fors V Mss.: sors B.', 'annis mss.: armis conjectured by Bouhier...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record manuscript variants explicitly and indicate conjectural emendations and their proponents. Where editors have proposed emendations (Bouhier, Bentley, Vollmer, etc.), report them and the manuscript support; compare external evidence and stylistic/contextual fit before adopting changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek minute/close analysis and consult specialist studies
rubrics_metrics.description: A minute analysis of this Satire is given by Charles Knapp in the Transactions of the American Philological Association, xlv. pp. 91 ff. For other attempts to improve the text see Knapp, loc. cit. pp. 102 ff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond general commentary, pursue close, line-by-line analysis and consult specialist articles and monographs (e.g., Knapp) that offer detailed textual and interpretive arguments; cite them when justifying editorial choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of poetic maturity vs immaturity
rubrics_metrics.description: Palmer thinks that this Satire 'was probably the last composed of those in the first book,' and Morris speaks of its 'maturity of style and treatment.' Campbell, however, points out 'distinct signs of immaturity,' such as the Lucretian echo in ll. 23-26, a passage which 'smacks of the novice in satire-writing', the weakness of l. 108, and the 'lame conclusion' in 11. 120, 121.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging the maturity of an individual poem, look for internal stylistic markers (originality vs. echoes of other authors, strength of individual lines, coherence and force of conclusion). Specific signs noted here include detectable echoes (e.g., Lucretius), weak or awkward lines, and a 'lame' or tacked-on conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of satiric type by tone and technique (Lucilian features)
rubrics_metrics.description: This immature and forbidding sketch, coarse and sensational in tone, and doubtless one of Horace's earliest efforts, is closely associated with the Lucilian type of satire. It abounds in personalities, freely handled, and Horace himself ... cites it later as an illustration of the kind of writing which had aroused enmity against the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify satiric poems by tone and technique: 'Lucilian' satire is characterized by coarseness, sensationalism, and frequent personal invective; such features signal a particular satiric tradition and help situate Horace's poem historically and stylistically (e.g., relation to Cynic philosophy and New Comedy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect and articulate intertextual influences and parallels
rubrics_metrics.description: Lejay has shown how dependent it ultimately is upon the erotic literature of the Hellenistic period as expressed in the popular Cynic philosophy, in the New Comedy, and in the Anthology. There is a striking parallel between it and a poem on love in the Oxyrhynchus Papyri by the Cynic Cercidas ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and document parallels and influences (Greek Hellenistic erotic poetry, Cynic thought, New Comedy, papyri parallels). Use such comparisons to explain motifs, diction, thematic emphases, and to date or contextualize passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic and moral criteria: 'golden mean' and avoidance of extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: one must not run to the other extreme, but should observe the golden mean ... There is modus in rebus, sunt certi denique fines, quos ultra citraque nequit consistere rectum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting Horace's moral stance, foreground the normative theme of moderation ('golden mean') as central: critique both extremes (avarice and prodigality, sensual excess and austerity) and treat thematic statements about measured behavior as key to understanding the poem's moral logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of illustrative exempla and anecdotes to develop rhetorical argument
rubrics_metrics.description: The poem uses comparative examples and anecdotes (the ant that stores for winter, Tantalus, Ummidius the miser, anecdotes of adulterers' fates) to demonstrate points about wealth, contentment, and vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In commentary and interpretation, analyze how Horace's exempla and short anecdotes function rhetorically to embody abstract morals; evaluate their selection, deployment, and effect on tone (didactic, ironic, satiric). Consider how such exempla support the poem's central arguments.
